title: Designs for Learning: Studying Science Museum Exhibits That Do More Than Entertain

findings.antecedent: Bike Cycle exhibit (complex machine, robotic simulation of bicycle rider, 4 buttons control pistons, requires right sequence and timing)
findings.mechanism: immediate apprehendability at the large scale (robot recognizable as person on bike) as well as the small scale (4 large buttons, color-coded)
findings.quote: 73% of visitors persisted until they had succeeded, and 70% said they thought the level of challenge was about right.

findings.antecedent: Downhill Race exhibit (racing wheels of different shape/weight down inclined plane, two lanes, six disks)
findings.consequent: visitor predictions, explanations, and new understandings
findings.mechanism: immediate apprehension that the exhibit involves racing the disks
findings.quote: several studies have shown that this exhibit provokes predictions, explanations, and new understandings that can be articulated

findings.antecedent: Frogs exhibit (tank with mini-ecosystem, nocturnal frogs hidden/sleeping)
findings.mechanism: visitors recognized the exhibit as an example of something where one had to wait and watch in order to be rewarded by a frog sighting
findings.quote: most likely of any in the exhibition to elicit complex inferences from visitors... None of the 30 pairs of visitors expressed frustration or annoyance

findings.antecedent: Frogs exhibit (tank with mini-ecosystem, nocturnal frogs hidden/sleeping)
findings.mechanism: recognized the exhibit as an example of something where one had to wait and watch
findings.quote: second most likely element to evoke stories and personal associations

findings.antecedent: Whodunit exhibition (framed by detective puzzle schema)
findings.consequent: visitor immediate apprehension of purpose and relationships of elements
findings.mechanism: familiar activities as over-arching schemas
findings.quote: allowed visitors to immediately apprehend the purpose and relationship of distinct elements

findings.antecedent: visitor comfort and orientation
findings.mechanism: lessens distracting stimuli and helps to put visitors within a comfortable framework from which to be curious.
findings.quote: visitors will only engage in a challenge if they are comfortable and oriented

findings.antecedent: pre-visit orientation (museum layout, store opportunities)
findings.mechanism: reduces the ever-present cognitive load on visitors, freeing them to focus on those aspects... worthy of their attention.
findings.quote: children on school field trips showed higher levels of learning if they were given a pre-visit orientation based on the layout of the museum

findings.antecedent: quieter, smaller, better-differentiated spaces
findings.mechanism: link the physical environment to learning through psychological processes such as cognitive fatigue, distraction, motivation, and anxiety
findings.quote: learning is enhanced in quieter, smaller, better-differentiated spaces.

limitations: Still need to know more about the impacts of apprehendability versus challenge, and the way in which the tension between them plays out at different scales in the museum visit, at different times, and with different audiences.
The field badly needs more studies of nonverbal forms of learning because these may be the dominant forms for a three-dimensional physical interaction, especially for children.

Nonverbal studies would also help to reveal the learning impacts of a controversial and increasingly common display technique we call “gratuitous interactivity,” where the interactive features of an exhibit are unrelated to its central phenomenon.
Large-scale design issues (conceptual coherence) are logistically difficult and expensive to test in real museum settings.

More research is needed to determine whether our instantiations of narrative have simply been flawed, or whether perhaps the chaotic, high-energy environment of a science museum and the nonanecdotal nature of science combine to make storytelling an ineffective strategy for learning in these settings.
We are unlikely to ever create generalizable enough design principles to obviate the need for research, prototyping, and evaluation.
